The mechanistic evidence for a direction-specific safety vulnerability is fundamentally weak. Control 1 shows a YELLOW verdict with a random_ratio of 0.445, meaning random directions achieve nearly half the effect of the extracted direction. This substantially undermines the claim that we've identified a specific, meaningful safety-relevant direction rather than a general sensitivity to perturbation in this layer's activation space. A mechanistically meaningful direction should show much stronger specificity (random_ratio < 0.2 would be more convincing).

More critically, Control 3 shows a 0% flip rate with a 10% degradation rate, earning a RED verdict. This is the most damning result from a mechanistic standpoint - the intervention produces no behavioral change on safety-relevant outputs while still causing some model degradation. This pattern suggests we're not manipulating a genuine safety circuit but rather introducing noise that occasionally disrupts coherent generation. A true mechanistic vulnerability would show reliable, direction-specific behavioral changes.

The GREEN verdict on Control 2 (coherence maintained) is actually concerning in this context - it means the intervention is subtle enough to preserve surface-level generation quality while failing to produce any measurable safety-relevant effect. This is consistent with the intervention being mechanistically inert for safety behaviors.
